screens.title: Custom Editor Tools & Editor Scripting
screens.subtitle: Make the Unity Editor work for your team — custom inspectors, windows, and menu actions.

narration.text: Editor scripting is about shaping your development environment so routine tasks are faster and safer. In this lesson you will learn why editor-only scripts are powerful, how they differ from runtime code, and how small tools like custom inspectors or an EditorWindow can save hours of repetitive work. We’ll use concrete examples: a custom inspector that tidies a player stats component, an EditorWindow that becomes a project tool, and a practical lab to build an inspector for a CollectibleItem. You will also see the attributes that make tools discoverable, like MenuItem and ContextMenu, and safety practices such as placing scripts inside an Editor folder and using serializedObject to preserve undo and serialization. By the end you’ll understand not just how to add UI to the Editor, but why you should: better workflows, fewer mistakes, and a smoother handoff between programmers and designers. As you learn, consider one repetitive task in your own project that could be automated with a small editor script — that will be your starting idea for practice.

keyIdea.title: Why Editor Scripting?
keyIdea.text: Editor scripts run only in the Unity Editor to automate workflows, enforce standards, and provide project-specific tooling without affecting builds.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate when to extend the Unity Editor and then implement those extensions safely. You will learn to create custom inspectors by inheriting from the Editor class, use serializedObject and ApplyModifiedProperties to ensure changes persist, and add actionable UI like buttons and sliders that designers can use. You will also build EditorWindows to host project tools and use MenuItem to surface them in the top menu, plus ContextMenu to add instance-level actions. Each objective focuses on practical skills: writing the right attribute, placing scripts in an Editor folder so they compile only for the editor, and using undo and set-dirty patterns so edits are reversible. For example, you’ll implement a CollectibleItem inspector that adds a duplicate action and a randomized value while keeping undo functionality. These skills reduce friction for designers and keep runtime builds lean because editor-only code is never included in the final game. Consider which part of your current workflow is most repetitive — that’s the first objective you should try to solve with an editor tool.

screens.title: What is Editor Scripting?
screens.subtitle: Definition, scope, and why it’s editor-only

narration.text: Editor scripting means writing C# code that modifies or extends the Unity Editor itself, not the runtime game. The key claim is simple: editor scripts execute only inside the Unity Editor and are excluded from builds when placed in an Editor folder. This separation matters because you can safely use editor-only APIs, diagnostic UI, and heavy tooling without affecting the shipped game. A concrete example is an EditorWindow that scans project assets and presents a dashboard of missing textures; this window never runs in the build. One common misconception is thinking editor scripts are 'just scripts' that can be mixed with runtime code. In practice, mixing them can cause compilation or runtime errors, because editor-only assemblies link to UnityEditor types that are absent in the player. Another practical contrast: a MonoBehaviour runs in play mode and affects gameplay, but an Editor script manipulates data, enforces standards, and provides shortcuts for designers. Why this matters: as projects scale, small editor tools remove repetitive clicks, reduce configuration mistakes, and let designers iterate faster. Reflect on a workflow you repeat often: could a window, a button, or a context action in the Inspector save minutes each time? That question will guide a useful first editor script.

keyIdea.title: Editor scripts are development-time tools
keyIdea.text: They run only in the Unity Editor, enabling automation and custom UI without affecting builds.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › What is Editor Scripting?
Definition
Editor scripting is writing C# that extends the Unity Editor UI and behavior. It uses UnityEditor APIs and runs only in the editor when stored in an Editor folder.
Why it matters
  • Automate repetitive tasks so designers iterate faster.
  • Enforce project standards and reduce human error.
  • Build bespoke workflows that match your game’s needs.
Common misconception
Editor scripts are not runtime code. Mixing editor-only assemblies with runtime code can create build errors because UnityEditor types are not available in players.
Concrete example
An EditorWindow that scans assets for missing references and displays a list for designers to fix. This window runs in the editor and is opened via a MenuItem.
Check your understanding
Name one repetitive workflow you do now and imagine a Button or EditorWindow that reduces it to one click. That idea is a valid first editor script.
Key Takeaway

Editor scripts are safe, powerful, and should be used to eliminate repetitive manual steps during development.

screens.title: Custom Inspectors — The workflow
screens.subtitle: Create, draw, and serialize safe changes

narration.text: A Custom Inspector lets you control how a MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject appears in Unity’s Inspector. The basic workflow is three steps: create a script in an Editor folder that inherits from Editor, decorate it with CustomEditor to target your type, and override OnInspectorGUI to draw controls. Start every OnInspectorGUI with serializedObject. Update to read the latest serialized values, and end with serializedObject. ApplyModifiedProperties to write back changes so Unity can serialize them and support undo. A concrete example is a PlayerStats editor that shows health and mana as sliders and uses PropertyField for experience and level. A common mistake is directly changing target fields without ApplyModifiedProperties, which causes edits to not persist or skip serialization hooks. Another issue is forgetting Undo. RecordObject when modifying scene objects from an editor action, which prevents undo. When drawing custom UI, prefer EditorGUILayout. PropertyField for properties you still want serialized defaults for, and use direct access only for runtime-only or calculated values. Try this: write a minimal CustomEditor for PlayerStats, put it in an Editor folder, then change a value and confirm it is saved after you hit play and stop. That confirmation proves serialization is working.

keyIdea.title: Three-step inspector pattern
keyIdea.text: Use CustomEditor, call serializedObject.Update, draw fields, and call ApplyModifiedProperties to persist and support undo.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Custom Inspectors
Step-by-step
  1. Create a C# script inside an Editor folder and inherit from UnityEditor.Editor.
  2. Add [CustomEditor(typeof(YourType))] and override OnInspectorGUI.
  3. Call serializedObject.Update(), draw PropertyFields or controls, and then serializedObject.ApplyModifiedProperties().
Quick rule
Always use serializedObject for editable properties to keep undo and prefab overrides working.
PlayerStats (visual)
// Inside PlayerStatsEditor.cs (Editor folder)
[CustomEditor(typeof(PlayerStats))]
public override void OnInspectorGUI() {
  serializedObject.Update();
  EditorGUILayout.IntSlider(...); // health/mana
  EditorGUILayout.PropertyField(serializedObject.FindProperty("experience"));
  if (GUILayout.Button("Grant 100 XP")) { player.GainExperience(100f); }
  serializedObject.ApplyModifiedProperties();
}
Example check: change experience, click ApplyModifiedProperties, and confirm the value persists after exiting play mode. If it doesn’t persist, inspect whether ApplyModifiedProperties was called or whether the property was modified directly on the target without serialization.

screens.title: PlayerStats Custom Inspector Example
screens.subtitle: Understand key lines and safety patterns

narration.text: Let’s walk through the PlayerStats example to see safe patterns in practice. The inspector script is placed in an Editor folder and tagged with CustomEditor to target PlayerStats. Inside OnInspectorGUI you begin with serializedObject. Update; this reads the serialized properties so PropertyField can draw them safely. Use EditorGUILayout. IntSlider for numeric ranges like health and mana to give designers an intuitive control. For some fields, like experience and level, PropertyField preserves prefab overrides and serialization semantics. When you add a button that calls player. GainExperience, remember that calling a public method on the target is acceptable for editor-time actions, but changes that affect scene objects should use Undo. RecordObject and EditorUtility. SetDirty so the change is undoable and marked dirty. Finally, call serializedObject. ApplyModifiedProperties to write back changes. A typical mistake is to set target fields directly and forget ApplyModifiedProperties; the result is values that appear changed but are not serialized, causing confusion when closing the editor. A quick test is to change a field, save the scene, restart the editor, and verify the value persisted. If it did, your inspector handled serialization correctly. Ask yourself: did I use PropertyField where prefab behavior matters and direct field access only for transient editor UI?

keyIdea.title: Test persistence
keyIdea.text: After implementing an inspector, change a value, restart Unity, and confirm the value persists to ensure you handled serialization and ApplyModifiedProperties.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › PlayerStats Inspector
Key lines explained
serializedObject.Update() — reads current serialized state so PropertyField shows accurate values.
EditorGUILayout.PropertyField — draws the property while keeping prefab and serialization behavior intact.
GUILayout.Button("Grant 100 XP") — triggers an editor-time action on the target; use with care for scene changes.
serializedObject.ApplyModifiedProperties() — writes changes back and ensures Unity serializes them and records them for undo.
Pro tip
Use PropertyField when you want to preserve prefab overrides; use direct access only for derived or editor-only fields.
Annotated snippet
serializedObject.Update();
// draw sliders
player.health = EditorGUILayout.IntSlider("Health", player.health, 0, 200);
EditorGUILayout.PropertyField(serializedObject.FindProperty("experience"));
if (GUILayout.Button("Grant 100 XP")) { player.GainExperience(100f); }
serializedObject.ApplyModifiedProperties();
Mini-check: after calling ApplyModifiedProperties, modify a value and use Undo to verify undo entry exists.

screens.title: EditorWindow: Building a project tool
screens.subtitle: Create, open, and interact with a custom window

narration.text: EditorWindows give you a free-form canvas to create project tools like a Quest Editor or Localization dashboard. The core pattern is to inherit from EditorWindow, implement OnGUI for UI, and add a static method with MenuItem to open it. In the example MyCustomWindow, a string field, a toggle group, and a button demonstrate typical UI. OnEnable and OnDisable let you initialize or release resources. Keep OnGUI efficient because it runs frequently; expensive work should be scheduled or done on user demand. A concrete exercise is to create a window that places prefabs in a grid: expose width, height, spacing, and a button that instantiates prefabs using Undo. RegisterCreatedObjectUndo so actions are undoable. A common misconception is treating EditorWindow like a MonoBehaviour lifecycle; it is a UI class with its own callbacks and should not assume play-mode behavior. Also, avoid referencing runtime-only classes directly from an Editor script; if you must manipulate runtime objects, do so via serializedObject or by getting scene GameObjects and recording undo. Finally, surface the window via MenuItem so team members can find it easily. Think: what dashboard would help your team’s daily work?

keyIdea.title: EditorWindow basics
keyIdea.text: Inherit from EditorWindow, implement OnGUI, and open via a MenuItem. Keep heavy work off continuous OnGUI passes and use Undo for created objects.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › EditorWindow
Essential pattern
Define a public class inheriting EditorWindow. Add a static ShowWindow method with MenuItem to open it. Implement OnGUI to draw the UI with EditorGUILayout and GUILayout calls.
Use OnEnable for initialization and avoid costly work inside OnGUI. For actions that create objects, use Undo.RegisterCreatedObjectUndo so creations are undoable.
Example use case
A Level Builder window that places prefab instances in a grid based on parameters, all created with Undo support.
MyCustomWindow snippet
[MenuItem("Cohortia Tools/My Custom Window")]
public static void ShowWindow() { GetWindow("Cohortia Tools"); }
void OnGUI() { GUILayout.Label("Settings", EditorStyles.boldLabel); myString = EditorGUILayout.TextField("Text Field", myString); if (GUILayout.Button("Perform Action")) { Debug.Log("Action performed"); } }
Mini-check: open the window from the menu, change parameters, press the action button, and confirm Undo works if the action creates scene objects.

narration.text: MenuItem and ContextMenu both expose editor actions, but they target different discovery patterns. MenuItem adds a command to Unity’s top menus, making tools globally available to the team. Use MenuItem for project-wide utilities such as opening a Level Builder, scanning assets, or running a batch operation. ContextMenu adds options to an individual component’s right-click menu or to a script’s inspector; it is ideal for instance-level actions like Reset Transform or Generate Collider for a selected object. A concrete example from the source: adding a MenuItem to open MyCustomWindow makes the tool discoverable to everyone via Tools → Cohortia Tools → My Custom Window. By contrast, ContextMenu is perfect when an action is only meaningful for a particular MonoBehaviour instance, like restoring a default configuration. A common misconception is exposing heavy, project-wide operations in a context menu; that hides tools from the expected menu structure and can confuse teammates. Decide based on scope and frequency: if the action helps many assets or global configuration, use MenuItem; if it helps a single component instance, use ContextMenu. Also remember both are editor-only attributes and belong on scripts inside Editor folders or on runtime scripts with context attributes where appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Scope decides attribute
keyIdea.text: Use MenuItem for global tools and EditorWindows; use ContextMenu for component instance actions visible in the inspector.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › MenuItem vs ContextMenu
MenuItem (global)
Add a MenuItem to expose EditorWindows and global utilities. Ideal for tools that operate across the project.
Example: [MenuItem("Cohortia Tools/My Custom Window")] opens an EditorWindow accessible from the top menu.
ContextMenu (instance)
Add per-component right-click actions. Use for instance-specific helpers like 'Duplicate Item' or 'Reset Settings'.
Example: a ContextMenu on a CollectibleItem could add 'Randomize Value' to the Inspector's context menu for the selected item.
Decision guide
  • If many assets or scenes need the tool, prefer MenuItem.
  • If the action applies only to a specific component instance, prefer ContextMenu.
  • Keep heavy operations behind confirmation and avoid firing them accidentally from a context click.

screens.title: CollectibleItem Inspector — Starter Code
screens.subtitle: Implement Duplicate and Randomize with undo and safety

narration.text: The CollectibleItem lab is a practical way to apply inspector and undo patterns. The runtime CollectibleItem holds an ItemType, a value, and a MeshRenderer reference. The editor script goes into an Editor folder and uses [CustomEditor(typeof(CollectibleItem))]. In the provided starter code you draw fields with PropertyField and add two buttons: Duplicate Item and Randomize Value. When duplicating, use Instantiate to create a copy, then call Undo. RegisterCreatedObjectUndo so the action is undoable. Also set Selection. activeGameObject to focus the new object for the designer. For randomizing the value, call Undo. RecordObject on the target before changing its value and then call EditorUtility. SetDirty on the object so Unity knows to save the change. Display a HelpBox warning if the MeshRenderer is null so designers see potential visibility issues. A common pitfall is changing the value without recording undo or setting dirty; such changes either won't be recorded in the undo stack or won't persist. After implementing, test by pressing Randomize, then pressing Cmd/Ctrl+Z to ensure undo works and restart Unity to confirm the randomized value persisted. That cycle demonstrates correct editor scripting practices for scene objects and designer-friendly tools.

keyIdea.title: Apply Undo correctly
keyIdea.text: Use Undo.RegisterCreatedObjectUndo for created objects and Undo.RecordObject + EditorUtility.SetDirty for property changes to ensure undo and persistence.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › CollectibleItem Inspector
Starter tasks
  • Draw type and value with PropertyField or specific controls.
  • Add a 'Duplicate Item' button that Instantiates and registers undo.
  • Add a 'Randomize Value' button that records undo and marks the object dirty.
  • Show a warning HelpBox if itemMeshRenderer is null.
Starter snippet (visual)
if (GUILayout.Button("Duplicate Item")) { var duplicate = Instantiate(item.gameObject, item.transform.position + Vector3.right, item.transform.rotation); Undo.RegisterCreatedObjectUndo(duplicate, "Duplicate Collectible Item"); Selection.activeGameObject = duplicate; }
if (GUILayout.Button("Randomize Value")) { Undo.RecordObject(item, "Randomize Collectible Value"); item.value = Random.Range(1, 101); EditorUtility.SetDirty(item); }
Warning handling
If itemMeshRenderer is null, draw a help box using EditorGUILayout.HelpBox to alert the designer that the item might not be visible in-scene.
Key Takeaway

Always combine Undo calls with EditorUtility.SetDirty when changing scene object properties so actions are undoable and persist.

screens.title: Editor-only compilation and folder rules
screens.subtitle: Where to place scripts and why it matters

narration.text: Editor scripts must be placed in a folder named Editor or a subfolder of it so Unity compiles them into editor-only assemblies. This rule keeps editor APIs out of runtime builds and avoids missing references in players. A concrete consequence: if you accidentally reference UnityEditor types from runtime code, your build will fail because those types are unavailable. Another important point is assembly boundaries: editor scripts compile separately, so they cannot be referenced by runtime assemblies. Use serializedObject to exchange data with runtime objects rather than trying to call into runtime types directly. In addition, follow undo and dirty patterns for scene edits: use Undo. RecordObject before changing an object's properties and call EditorUtility. SetDirty to mark the object for saving. Performance awareness is also part of safety. OnGUI is called multiple times per frame in the editor; don’t run expensive logic there. Cache results, use EditorApplication. update for polling or schedule heavy operations behind user actions. The bottom line is discipline: proper folder placement, serialization patterns, undo handling, and performance mindfulness make editor tools reliable and safe for team use.

keyIdea.title: Editor folder rule
keyIdea.text: Place editor scripts in an Editor folder to ensure they compile only for the editor and do not end up in runtime builds.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Compilation & Safety
Editor folder and assemblies
Scripts inside a folder named Editor compile only for the Unity Editor. This prevents UnityEditor APIs from being included in runtime builds and avoids missing-type errors. Because editor code compiles into separate assemblies, runtime code cannot depend on editor-only assemblies.
Undo and persistence
  • Use Undo.RecordObject before changing scene objects.
  • Call EditorUtility.SetDirty after modifying objects so changes are saved.
  • Test Undo and persistence by performing actions and using undo, then restarting the editor.
Performance
OnGUI is called frequently. Avoid expensive operations there. Use event-driven patterns or schedule heavy tasks on demand.
Misconception
Putting an editor script outside an Editor folder will not magically exclude UnityEditor types from the build; it causes compilation issues.

narration.text: A hallmark of production-ready editor tools is correct undo behavior and persistence. Use Undo. RecordObject before mutating a component or asset so the action appears in the undo stack. For object creation, use Undo. RegisterCreatedObjectUndo so creation can be reverted. When you change values on scene objects or assets, call EditorUtility. SetDirty afterward so Unity marks them for saving. With prefabs and serialized properties, prefer serializedObject and PropertyField to maintain prefab overrides and connect to Unity’s serialization system. A concrete example: randomizing a CollectibleItem value must be wrapped by Undo. RecordObject and followed by EditorUtility. SetDirty, otherwise the random value may not be saved or undoable. A common mistake is calling Undo. RecordObject but forgetting SetDirty, which makes the change undoable in the session but not persisted to disk. Another pitfall is changing nested prefab data incorrectly; always use the property system or record and apply property changes via serializedObject. Test each action: perform the editor action, press undo, and restart the editor to confirm persistence. These checks ensure your tool behaves like first-class editor functionality. Undo, EditorUtility.SetDirty, and Prefabs means record undo for changes and call setdirty to ensure actions are both reversible and saved across editor restarts.. In practical terms, making changes reversible and persistent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify undo + persistence
keyIdea.text: Record undo for changes and call SetDirty to ensure actions are both reversible and saved across editor restarts.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Undo & Persistence
Patterns
  • Undo.RecordObject(object, "Action") — use before property changes.
  • Undo.RegisterCreatedObjectUndo(newObj, "Create") — use when instantiating objects.
  • EditorUtility.SetDirty(object) — call after changes to ensure saving.
Quick test
Perform an edit, undo, and then restart the editor to confirm persistence and undo behavior.
Prefab note
When editing prefab properties, prefer serializedObject to correctly maintain overrides and prefab connections rather than directly changing nested values.
Common mistake

Forgetting EditorUtility.SetDirty after Undo.RecordObject can lead to non-persistent changes.

screens.title: Designing designer-friendly inspectors
screens.subtitle: Grouping, HelpBox warnings, and action placement

narration.text: Good inspectors are about usability. Group related fields with BeginVertical or foldouts so designers can focus, and use labels that communicate intent. Add HelpBox warnings for misconfigurations such as missing references. Place action buttons where they are discoverable but not harmful — for instance, put a Duplicate Item button near the top and a Randomize Value action behind a small confirmation if it has wide impact. Use sliders for bounded numeric values and PropertyField for properties you want Unity to manage. A practical example: in a Weapon inspector you might group Combat Stats and Ammo settings in two collapsible sections, show a HelpBox when fireRate is extremely high, and add a Test Fire button that triggers a safe validation rather than playing the weapon. One misconception is adding too many buttons: each action should have a clear, repeatable purpose. Finally, document what an action does in a tooltip or HelpBox so other team members understand the consequences. These small ergonomics make tools approachable and reduce accidental misuse. Designing designer-friendly inspectors means organize fields, use helpbox warnings, and place actions thoughtfully so inspectors are safe and approachable for designers.. In practical terms, grouping, helpbox warnings, and action placement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Usability matters
keyIdea.text: Organize fields, use HelpBox warnings, and place actions thoughtfully so inspectors are safe and approachable for designers.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Designer-friendly Inspectors
Layout patterns
  • Group fields by purpose with foldouts or BeginVertical blocks.
  • Use sliders for ranges, PropertyField for serialized properties, and custom draws for complex data.
  • Provide action buttons with clear labels and optional confirmation for destructive operations.
Example
Group Combat Stats and Ammo, display a HelpBox if fireRate exceeds a safe threshold, and provide a Test Fire button that runs a safe validation method.
HelpBox examples
Use EditorGUILayout.HelpBox("Message", MessageType.Warning) to surface issues clearly. Include suggested fixes where possible.
Key Takeaway

Make inspectors clear and safe. Designers should understand the impact of each control without asking a programmer.

screens.title: Assessment & Live coding brief
screens.subtitle: From cluttered inspector to polished tool — a guided plan

narration.text: For assessment, convert a cluttered PlayerSettings or Weapon inspector into a polished custom inspector and build an EditorWindow tool reachable from the menu. Start by identifying groups of related fields and create foldouts. Implement sliders and property drawing to restore prefab behavior. Add at least two actions: one instance-level button like Duplicate Item and one global tool such as a Level Builder window opened via MenuItem. Ensure all changes use serializedObject. ApplyModifiedProperties, Undo. RecordObject or Undo. RegisterCreatedObjectUndo, and EditorUtility. SetDirty where needed. A recommended live coding sequence is: 1) show the default, cluttered inspector, 2) create an Editor folder and new inspector script, 3) implement Update/ApplyModifiedProperties flow, 4) add HelpBox warnings for invalid values, 5) create a simple EditorWindow and open it via MenuItem, and 6) test undo and persistence. Common mistakes to cover in the demo are forgetting ApplyModifiedProperties and not registering undo for created objects. End the session by asking learners to pick one repetitive task from their project to automate as a next step. In practical terms, from cluttered inspector to polished tool — a guided plan. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Before you close this chapter, commit three short concepts to memory. First, Editor Scripting is for development-time workflows and must be placed in an Editor folder so it does not affect builds. Second, Custom Inspectors should use serializedObject. Update and ApplyModifiedProperties, and use PropertyField to preserve prefab behavior. Third, always make editor changes undoable with Undo. RecordObject or Undo. RegisterCreatedObjectUndo and call EditorUtility. SetDirty to persist changes. These rules ensure your tools are reliable, discoverable, and safe for your team to use. As you build your first tool, test persistence and undo thoroughly. That testing habit separates fragile prototypes from tools you can confidently include in your project pipeline. Key Concepts means editor folder placement, serializedobject patterns, and proper undo/persist methods are the core practices for editor tooling.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three rules to follow
keyIdea.text: Editor folder placement, serializedObject patterns, and proper undo/persist methods are the core practices for editor tooling.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Key Concepts
Editor-only
Place scripts in an Editor folder so they compile only for the editor and not the build.
Serialized properties
Use serializedObject.Update and ApplyModifiedProperties for safe serialization and prefab support.
Undo & Persist
Record undo and call EditorUtility.SetDirty for reversible, saved changes.
Summary

Follow these three core practices to make editor tools that are safe, discoverable, and useful to your team.

narration.text: Keep a short checklist when you build editor tools. First, put scripts in an Editor folder. Second, prefer serializedObject and PropertyField when editing properties to keep Unity’s serialization and prefab behaviors intact. Third, make all changes undoable and persistent with Undo calls and EditorUtility. SetDirty. Fourth, expose tools using MenuItem for global utilities and ContextMenu for instance actions. Finally, test performance by avoiding heavy logic in OnGUI. These reminders help you ship editor tools that your teammates trust and use every day. As a closing prompt, think of one small editor improvement you can implement in the next thirty minutes and make it undoable and menu-accessible. What to Remember means editor folder, serializedobject, undo+setdirty, menuitem/contextmenu, avoid heavy ongui work.. In practical terms, short reminders for daily use. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
